newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Mexico, EU take step toward free trade.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mexico, EU take step toward free trade.

text.p: Mexico may have to wait until the next century for free trade with the European Union (EU) despite an accord between the two sides that paves the way for direct negotiations, the EU ambassador to Mexico said on Wednesday.
Earlier, Mexico and the European Union signed an interim accord that allows Mexico negotiate a trade agreement directly with the EU rather than the parliaments of each of its member countries.
"We not only have the possibility (of free trade) but the authorization to negotiate. We have a fast track for Mexico," Ambassador Jacques Lecomte told Reuters in an interview.
To be sure, he cautioned, negotiations could go slowly.

"The free-trade agreements will probably not be before the end of the century," Lecomte said. "It will probably be in October when the (European) Commission will present to the European Union a decision to start negotiations of the commercial side that will probably intitiate by April or May of next year."

Any free-trade pact would have less of an impact than the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), he said, because of trade among Canada, Mexico and the United States is much larger than trade between Mexico and the EU.
Trade between Mexico and the EU reached $11.28 billion in 1996, accounting for 6.1 percent of Mexico's total. Mexico has run a trade deficit with the EU for at least six years.

Its principal exports to the EU in 1996 were crude oil, large engines, computer parts, garbanzos, honey and beer. From the EU, Mexico imported powdered milk, vehicle parts and accessories, medicines and textile machinery.
Trade issues are only part of the EU-Mexico accord, which also seeks to promote a more open political dialogue and business cooperation.
"The concept of the idea is larger (than NAFTA) because it has a political side and a cooperation side, helping Mexico develop and coordinating between medium and smaller companies," he said.
